title: The Glue Guy: How Josh Hart Found His Calling in New York
thumb_prompt: A worn basketball resting on a Madison Square Garden court with orange and blue tape wrapped around it, documentary lighting with soft shadows, archival photograph aesthetic
thumb_subject: a versatile guard in a blue number three Knicks jersey diving for a loose ball, shown in silhouette

paragraphs.text: February eighth, twenty twenty three. Most Knicks fans do not remember this date. They remember the Mikal Bridges trade. They remember the Karl Anthony Towns blockbuster. They remember the day Jalen Brunson left money on the table. But February eighth, twenty twenty three, changed everything. That was the day the Portland Trail Blazers sent Josh Hart to New York for Cam Reddish, Ryan Arcidiacono, Svi Mykhailiuk, and a protected first round pick. It was barely a headline. Hart was averaging nine and a half points for a rebuilding Blazers team. He was on his fourth franchise in six seasons.

Three years later, Josh Hart has an NBA championship ring. Portland has Kris Murray, who is shooting under thirty percent from three. The Knicks have a player who logged thirty nine minutes in the championship clincher. A player who grabbed fifteen rebounds in Game One of the Finals while scoring just three points. A player who Tom Thibodeau trusted with his life. This is not a story about statistics. This is a story about identity. About finding the one place where your specific skill set becomes indispensable.

Hart arrived in New York in February twenty twenty three and immediately made the kind of impact that does not show up on highlight reels. He shot fifty eight percent from the floor in twenty five regular season games. More importantly, he shot fifty one point nine percent from three. That is not sustainable, and everyone knew it. But what was sustainable was the rebounding. The screening. The deflections. The willingness to guard four positions. Hart played himself into a four year, eighty one million dollar extension by August. That contract looked like an overpay to some. Today it looks like highway robbery.

Look at his playoff résumé with the Knicks. Fifty six postseason games. Forty six starts. He has been in the Knicks playoff rotation for four consecutive springs. In the twenty twenty six championship run, he averaged ten point four points, eight point nine rebounds, four point six assists, and one point seven steals. Those are not All Star numbers. But here is what matters. The Knicks were outscored by twenty two points in Game One of the Finals when Hart sat. They outscored San Antonio by twenty two when he played. He was a plus minus hero without ever dominating the ball.

Josh Hart became the first Knick since two thousand four to average over forty two minutes per game in a single postseason. Think about that. Not since the Allan Houston era has a Knick logged those kinds of minutes in the playoffs. He played every single minute of multiple games. Thirty nine minutes in the championship clincher. Thirty seven point six minutes per game across the entire twenty twenty five regular season. Tom Thibodeau gets criticized for his minute management. With Hart, it was not about overuse. It was about necessity. When Hart sat, the Knicks bled possessions.

This durability is not new. Hart missed only twelve regular season games across three years with the Knicks. He has played through bumps and bruises that would sideline lesser competitors. He fractured his left ring finger this past summer and was back working on his three point shot within weeks. The man does not take maintenance days. He does not load manage. In an era where stars rest for back to backs and minor ailments, Hart is an anachronism. He is proof that availability is the best ability. The Knicks won a championship because their best players were always on the floor.

His role evolved dramatically under Mike Brown this past season. After Thibodeau was let go, many wondered if Hart's minutes would crater. Instead, Brown found new ways to deploy him. Hart started games. He came off the bench in crucial playoff moments. He guarded primary scorers. He ran point when Brunson needed a breather. The versatility became his calling card. He is listed as a shooting guard but has played small forward and power forward extensively. At six foot five, he averaged eight point two rebounds with Portland. That led the entire NBA for players his height or shorter.

There is a specific skill that separates Hart from other role players. Screening. He sets the kind of picks that free up Jalen Brunson and Karl Anthony Towns for clean looks. In Game Four of the Finals, he had two screen assists. That means two times his screen directly led to a made basket. He contests shots without fouling. He recovers loose balls. He makes the right pass ninety nine percent of the time. These are not glamorous skills. They are championship skills. The Knicks outscored opponents by fourteen point nine points per one hundred possessions in the playoffs. Hart was the connective tissue.

You cannot tell Josh Hart's Knicks story without Jalen Brunson. They won a national championship together at Villanova in twenty sixteen. Hart scored fifteen points per game in that NCAA tournament. Brunson was the point guard running the show. They learned under Jay Wright how to win without always stuffing the stat sheet. That philosophy became the foundation of this Knicks championship. When Hart was traded to New York in February twenty twenty three, he was reuniting with his college backcourt partner. That chemistry was immediate. They spoke the same basketball language. They trusted each other implicitly.

Brunson took a massive pay cut to keep this core together. He left one hundred thirteen million dollars on the table. That sacrifice set the tone. It said championships matter more than individual wealth. Hart embodied that same mentality. He never complained about minutes distribution. He never lobbied for more shots. When Mike Brown asked him to come off the bench in the twenty twenty five Eastern Conference Finals, Hart agreed immediately. He told reporters it was his decision. He was comfortable with it. That is leadership. That is ego suppression in service of winning.

The Villanova pipeline runs deep in this Knicks organization. Mikal Bridges is another Wright disciple. Donte DiVincenzo was part of the core before being traded for Towns. These players share a common basketball philosophy. They cut hard. They screen. They rotate defensively. They do not need the ball to make an impact. Wright built a college dynasty by recruiting unselfish players and teaching them to maximize possessions. The Knicks imported that culture wholesale. It is not a coincidence that their championship coincided with the Villanova reunion reaching critical mass.

Hart holds the Knicks franchise record for most triple doubles in a single season. Six. That puts him ahead of some franchise legends in that specific category. He became only the third Knick ever to play all forty eight minutes in a regular season game, joining Clyde Frazier and Jerry Lucas. Think about that company. Frazier is a Hall of Famer and the face of Knicks basketball. Lucas was a genius on the court. Hart is carving out his own legacy, one that prioritizes durability and versatility. His nickname with fans is Ironman. It fits perfectly.

Josh Hart was never supposed to be a star. Utah drafted him thirtieth overall in twenty seventeen and immediately traded him to the Lakers. He spent two seasons in Los Angeles, mostly coming off the bench. Then New Orleans. Then Portland. Each stop felt temporary. He was the kind of player teams traded when they needed to match salaries or acquire draft picks. In Portland, he started fifty one games and averaged nine and a half points. The Blazers were rebuilding. Damian Lillard's era was ending. Hart did not fit the timeline. So they shipped him out for a lottery protected pick and Cam Reddish.

That Portland trade haunts the Blazers now. Reddish played twenty nine total games for them and was not brought back. Svi Mykhailiuk never suited up. The first round pick became Kris Murray, who has not reached thirty percent from three in any of his three seasons. Meanwhile, Hart just won a championship. He played thirty nine minutes in the clincher. He logged thirteen points and eleven rebounds. The Blazers bet on potential. The Knicks bet on production. That is the difference between rebuilding and winning. Hart always had the tools. He needed the right organization to unlock them.

What changed in New York? The role clarity. Thibodeau and then Brown gave Hart a defined mission. Rebound. Defend. Screen. Move the ball. Do not worry about scoring unless the shot is wide open. That simplicity freed him. In Portland, he was asked to be a secondary scorer on a team going nowhere. In New York, he was asked to be the glue. The connective tissue between stars. Hart thrived in that role because it matched his skill set perfectly. He is not a shot creator. He is a winning player. There is a massive difference.

Look at his Finals performance for proof. Game One, he scored three points on one of five shooting. He also grabbed fifteen rebounds, dished six assists, swiped four steals, and was plus twenty two. Game Five, the clincher, he scored thirteen points and grabbed eleven boards in thirty nine minutes. The scoring was inconsistent across the series. The impact never wavered. San Antonio shot two for eight from three when Hart was the primary defender in Game Four. He contested seven shots that game. Those numbers do not make SportsCenter. They make championships.

sections.heading: The Blueprint for Modern Role Players

paragraphs.text: Josh Hart is the blueprint for the modern role player. He does not need the ball. He does not need plays called for him. He makes his teammates better by doing the dirty work. Every championship team has a player like this. Draymond Green with the Warriors. PJ Tucker with the Bucks. Shane Battier with the Heat. These are not household names to casual fans. They are legends to people who understand winning basketball. Hart fits that mold perfectly. He sacrifices his body. He plays through pain. He never takes possessions off. That consistency is rare.

The Knicks offseason has been quiet so far. They lost Mitchell Robinson to Boston. They signed Andre Drummond for center depth. They brought back Jose Alvarado, Landry Shamet, and Jordan Clarkson on team friendly deals. The core remains intact. That includes Hart, who is under contract through twenty twenty seven. His deal pays him roughly twenty million per season. That is a bargain for a player who can guard multiple positions, rebound like a big man, and play forty minutes without breaking down. The second apron makes contracts like his even more valuable. He provides All Star impact at role player cost.

Training camp opens in late September. The Knicks will face the Raptors twice in preseason and likely the Sixers with LeBron James. Those games do not matter for standings. They matter for rhythm. For Hart, the preseason is about maintaining his conditioning. He does not need to prove anything. He has a championship ring. He has the respect of his coaches and teammates. He has found his home. After bouncing around four teams in six seasons, Hart finally has stability. New York is not trading him. They are building around him. That security allows him to focus purely on winning.

The Knicks won their first championship in fifty three years. That drought defined a generation of fans. It created a narrative that New York could not win in the modern NBA. Josh Hart helped shatter that narrative. He was not the leading scorer. He was not the Finals MVP. But he was indispensable. Every title team needs a player willing to do the unglamorous work. Hart embraced that role completely. His legacy in New York is already secure. He is the glue guy who helped bring a championship back to Madison Square Garden. That is enough. That is everything.

February eighth, twenty twenty three. Remember that date. It was the day the Knicks acquired the final piece of their championship puzzle. It was not a blockbuster. It was not headline news. It was Josh Hart for Cam Reddish and a protected pick. Three and a half years later, it is one of the most important trades in franchise history. Hart found his calling in New York. He found a role that maximized his skill set. He found a team that valued his contributions. And the Knicks found their glue guy. Sometimes the quietest moves make the loudest impact. This is that story.
